Below, trend graphs (CPU, memory, network, disk I/O, free space) are kept as history via RRD in a bounded file that never grows. Four ranges: Hour / Day / Week / Month.

blocks.caption: The Monitoring page: host gauges, RRD graphs and Claude usage.

blocks.text: An account filter (“All” + one chip per subscription) and a range selector show incoming/outgoing tokens, cost and the number of active sessions, kept as history by RRD. For a specific account, the plan limits (5H and weekly windows, in %) are also plotted.

items: Ollama supervision: real-time status, models loaded in RAM (unloadable), installed models.
Sessions: memory, CPU and log size per live session (4 s poll).

en.title: Tools configuration
en.tagline: Telegram, Proxmox, Home Assistant, Synology NAS, Email, S3 and Infomaniak DNS connectors.

blocks.text: The Tools page is driven by a catalog: each connector type exposes its own configuration fields. Secrets (passwords, tokens, keys) are encrypted at rest and are never returned by the API. A “Test” button validates the configuration, even before saving.

blocks.caption: The Tools page: available connectors and configured instances.

items: Telegram: bot token + chat_id (assisted chat detection and a test message).

Proxmox: URL, credentials, unverified-TLS option; a supervision dashboard (VMs, resources); snapshots (create / rollback / delete); VM backups via vzdump to any configured storage (proxmox_backup_vm, proxmox_list_storages); a read-only backup health report (proxmox_backup_report, see below).
Home Assistant: instance URL + Long-Lived Access Token (unverified-TLS option). List entities, read a state, call a service (light.turn_on, climate.set_temperature…), turn on/off.
Synology NAS: DSM URL + credentials. System information, volumes, shared folders, HyperBackup tasks (list and trigger).
Email (SMTP): server, port, credentials, sender; sending with attachments. This is the connector that ships the PDF manual.
S3: endpoint, bucket, access keys, region; a dashboard (buckets, usage). Uploading/downloading objects, plus public upload (ACL public-read) that returns a direct, non-presigned URL.

Infomaniak DNS: Infomaniak API token (Manager → Developer → API Keys). List, create, update and delete DNS records on your Infomaniak domains (A, AAAA, CNAME, TXT, MX…). Enables Let's Encrypt certificates via DNS-01 challenge and subdomain management for containers.

GitHub: Personal Access Token (scope repo). List repositories, create a repository (public or private), and push a local directory backup to GitHub (github_push_backup — creates the repo if missing, commits and force-pushes).

Nginx Proxy Manager: instance URL + admin account. List, create, enable/disable and delete proxy hosts; list certificates and access lists. With ssl=true a Let's Encrypt certificate (HTTP-01 challenge) is requested for the domain, which must therefore already point to NPM.

IMAP (email): server, port, credentials; read-only (mailboxes with counters, list, search, reading with the attachment list, without marking as read). Towards a remote server TLS is mandatory and the certificate is verified. For Proton mail, add nothing by hand: use the “Proton Bridge — mail” panel at the top of the page (see below).

Proton Bridge — mail (panel at the top of the Tools page): click “Connect mail (Proton Bridge)”, enter the Proton address and password, then the 2FA code (and the mailbox password if your account uses two passwords). The Hub drives Proton Bridge on this server, adds the account, reads the IMAP password Bridge generated and creates the “Proton Bridge” IMAP instance by itself (127.0.0.1, local TLS), open to the assistant. Your Proton password and codes are never stored, logged or sent back to the browser; only Bridge's IMAP password is kept, encrypted. The panel shows the state (Bridge running, account added, synchronisation, last error) and a “Disconnect from Bridge” button. One sign-in attempt per click, never retried automatically; an anti-abuse block is shown as is with the way forward and a 15-minute pause. If Proton requires human verification (CAPTCHA, right at the password, i.e. before the 2FA step), the panel shows, in a dedicated block, the verification link Bridge provides (clickable, with a “Copy link” button; nothing opens automatically): open it in your own browser, solve the CAPTCHA, then click “I solved the CAPTCHA, continue” (the attempt stays open for 10 minutes); only then does the panel ask for the 2FA code. “Cancel” cleanly abandons the attempt: the Bridge session is killed without sending anything to Proton. A refused or repeated CAPTCHA stops the operation without retry (15-minute pause). Outside waits for you, the panel never spins for more than ~2 min. Bridge restarts for a few seconds during the operation. Read-only: sending mail (Bridge SMTP) is not exposed.

Proton Calendar (read, and write of simple events: create, update, delete; no recurring events or guests; the assistant always asks for your confirmation before writing): enter the username, save, then “Connect the account” in the Proton session panel (password, then the 2FA code if the account has one). The password and code are never kept: only the session is stored, encrypted, and refreshed without logging in again. If Proton refuses the session (anti-abuse block, code 2028…), the connector pauses with a growing delay (15 min to 24 h) and does not retry; lift the block on the Proton side then reconnect the account. If Proton requires human verification (CAPTCHA, code 9001), the panel shows a dedicated block with the verify.proton.me link given by the API (clickable, “Copy link” button, nothing opens automatically): open it in your own browser, solve the CAPTCHA, then click “I solved the CAPTCHA, continue”; the Hub then sends the sign-in once more to Proton with the verified token, then moves on to the 2FA code. Your password stays in the server's memory only during this wait (10 minutes at most), never stored or logged; “Cancel” sends nothing to Proton and wipes it. Waiting for the CAPTCHA triggers no pause; only a real refusal (CAPTCHA rejected or asked again) does, and during a pause the “Sign in” button sends nothing. Mail no longer goes through this connector (see IMAP). If Proton answers “Invalid app version” (code 5002/5003) this is not an account block: no pause is applied; the application identity sent to Proton (default external-drive-claude_hub@1.0.0) is set in the tool's advanced “Application identity” field, or with the HUB_PROTON_APP_VERSION environment variable.

WhatsApp: QR-code pairing, sending and reading messages. In bot mode each conversation opens a Claude session; restrict senders with the allowed-numbers list, preferably in international format (+41791234567), which is matched exactly.

blocks.text: These connectors are also exposed as tools to Claude sessions (telegram_send_message, proxmox_list_vms, proxmox_backup_vm, ha_call_service, synology_info, email_send, s3_*, infomaniak_list_dns_records, infomaniak_create_dns_record, github_list_repos, github_push_backup, etc.).

Configured tools are grouped by category (Home, Messaging, Mail & calendar, Infrastructure, Scripts & status, Assistant & Hub, Other). Each connector type has a default category assigned automatically; a new connector type with no known category goes into “Other”. Every section can be collapsed (remembered in the browser) and the search box filters by tool name, connector type or action name/description (e.g. “backup” finds Proxmox; matching actions are shown on the card).

items: “Organise” button: move a tool (the “Category” menu under the card; “Automatic” puts it back in its type's default category), create a category, rename it (empty name = translated default label), delete it (its tools return to automatic; “Other” cannot be deleted) and reorder the sections (↑ ↓, order stored server-side, shared by all devices).

API: GET/POST /api/tool-categories, PATCH/DELETE /api/tool-categories/{id}, PUT /api/tool-categories/order {ids}, and PATCH /api/tools/{id} {category} ("" = automatic). Each tool exposes category (effective category) and categoryAuto; the /api/tools/connectors catalogue lists each connector's actions.

blocks.text: “Organising” means filing under categories: it is presentation only, a category changes nothing about permissions or behaviour. Classification is per configured tool (card): script_* and hub_* actions belong to the “Claude Hub” connector and therefore follow its category.

The proxmox_backup_report tool (read-only, same credentials as the Proxmox connector) queries the API live: it lists every VM and container on every node (including ones created later, with nothing to configure), reads the scheduled backup jobs and their selections, the vzdump tasks of the window (scheduled or manual, status, duration, log excerpt on error) and the usage of backup storages. It flags: guests never backed up or whose last backup exceeds the threshold (max(window, job period + 12 h)), guests covered by no active job, failures and warnings, low space (< 10 %, critical < 5 %), unreachable node or API. A successful manual backup never hides a failed scheduled job. Parameters: hours (window, default 36), node, storage. Text received from Proxmox is treated as data (truncated, never interpreted).

Every Monday at 06:00 UTC (08:00 Swiss summer time, 07:00 in winter: the scheduler runs in UTC) an assistant automation (Automations tab, “Rapport hebdo des sauvegardes Proxmox (lundi matin)”) calls the tool and sends you a short WhatsApp report: one line when all is well, otherwise the list of problems. It replaces the old Telegram task (Tasks › “Rapport hebdo des backups Proxmox (Telegram)”, disabled but kept with its script ~/.local/share/system/backup-monitor.sh: re-enable it with the switch on the Tasks page).

The Cloudflare connector lists zones, manages DNS records, Cloudflare Tunnels (outbound connection from the server, no port to open) and Access applications (which protect a public hostname behind an e-mail sign-in). It does not replace the Infomaniak connector: it only sees domains whose DNS zone is hosted at Cloudflare.

items: Cloudflare › Manage Account › Account API Tokens (or My Profile › API Tokens) › Create Token › Create Custom Token. Name: “claude-hub”.

Minimal permissions (add only what you need): Zone › Zone › Read (always); Zone › DNS › Edit (DNS); account-level Zone › Zone › Edit (add a domain); Zone › DNSSEC › Edit (DNSSEC); Account › Cloudflare Tunnel › Edit (tunnels); Account › Access: Apps and Policies › Edit (Access applications); optional Account › Access: Organizations, Identity Providers, and Groups › Read (list sign-in methods).
Resources: Account → your account only; Zone → “Specific zone” → the one domain concerned (never “All zones”). Tick no “API Tokens” permission and no “User” level one.
Optional but advised: client IP filtering (the Hub's public IP) and an expiry date (e.g. 90 days). Create it and copy the token (shown once).
Hub › Tools › Cloudflare: paste the token, leave “Allow changes” unticked for read-only, save, then “Test”. The account id is only needed if the token sees several accounts.

To change things: tick “Allow changes” and save. Every change asks for a confirmation naming the exact change and is written to the Journal (Journal tab, kept 1 year). “Forget the token” removes it from the Hub; also delete it at Cloudflare.

blocks.text: Zones and DNSSEC: cloudflare_create_zone adds a domain (Free plan, hosted DNS) without importing anything or changing name servers — the result lists the assigned name servers; cloudflare_get_zone_status re-reads the state (pending/active); cloudflare_get_dnssec, cloudflare_enable_dnssec and cloudflare_disable_dnssec read, turn on and turn off DNSSEC signing and give the DS record (key tag, algorithm, digest type, digest) to publish at the registrar. Creating a zone needs the token to cover all zones of the account: grant that only while adding. Only disable DNSSEC after removing the DS at the registrar. MX (priority), SRV (“priority weight port target”) and CAA (“flags tag value”) records are supported. Assistant: the cloudflare_list_* tools are read-only. Write tools (cloudflare_create/update/delete_dns_record, _tunnel, _set_tunnel_routes, _access_app) need “Allow changes” AND user_confirmed=true after your explicit approval; they are never exposed to the remote Claude connector. A tunnel's install token is never given to the assistant: it is only shown on this page, after confirmation.

Everything the API returns (names, comments, TXT values) is treated as untrusted data. Publishing a hostname through a tunnel exposes it to the Internet: always create the matching Access application (only the listed e-mails get in); the Hub warns about a published hostname with no Access application.

The Hub's DNS operations (the record created when a domain is added, the DNS-01 challenge of Let's Encrypt certificates) go through a “DNS provider” chosen per zone. Without a setting a zone uses Infomaniak. The setting is in Tools › Infomaniak DNS or Cloudflare › “DNS provider per zone”.

items: Only switch a zone to Cloudflare AFTER its name servers were changed at the registrar and the zone was checked (script deploy/cloudflare/compare-zone.sh): the Hub never touches name servers.
Enter the zone (e.g. example.com), pick the provider (it needs an active connector), “Apply” and confirm. The change is written to the Journal. Rollback: set Infomaniak the same way.
“Simulate” (dry-run) shows what the Hub would do (calls, record, acme.sh hook) without sending anything and without a token.

blocks.text: At Cloudflare, records created by the Hub are always “DNS only” (grey cloud) and need “Allow changes” on the Cloudflare connector. The certificate challenge uses the token directly (Zone › DNS › Edit permission) and is written to the Journal.

Skills are reusable Claude Code capabilities, shared across projects and across all subscriptions. The Skills page lets you create one (guided authoring) or discover/install an existing one (web search), and evolve, validate or disable them.

blocks.caption: The skills library.

blocks.text: The global RAG offers several named bases. You add documents to them (a file, a web link, pasted text) which are chunked and vectorized (local embeddings via Ollama, SQLite vector store). Sessions query these bases through an MCP tool. Each project also has a private RAG base, indexed automatically on its code.

blocks.caption: The grid of RAG knowledge bases.

blocks.text: Inside a base, click a document's title (or “view”) to display the text that was actually indexed — handy to check the extraction of a PDF or a web page. The preview is capped at 500 KB.

en.title: Configuration & subscriptions
en.tagline: Runtime settings, themes and Claude accounts.

blocks.text: The Configuration page adjusts the default permission mode, the Claude model (an Opus / Sonnet / Haiku dropdown — picking Sonnet or Haiku uses less usage quota than Opus), the maximum number of turns, the idle timeout and the resource caps. These settings apply to new sessions; running sessions keep their own. This is also where you pick the color theme. The model set here is the global default: each project can override it (project page, "Model"), and each session can pick its model at launch ("Model for next session") — this is the hybrid workflow: e.g. Sonnet by default, Opus case by case. The model is fixed for the whole lifetime of a session (a session does not switch models mid-run).

blocks.caption: The Configuration page.

blocks.text: DNS server IP: the address published in the A records created for containers. Three modes — local IP (detected LAN address), public IP (fetched dynamically, refreshed hourly) or custom IP. In local or public mode, if detection fails, domain provisioning is refused with an error rather than publishing a wrong address.

Several Anthropic subscriptions can be connected, with statistics isolated per subscription. Connecting is done entirely in the browser (an authorization URL, then a code to paste) or via an API key. A first account can already be linked during the initial setup wizard. One account is set as “default”; each project can override the account it uses.
An automatic safeguard pauses a subscription's sessions when its 5H window reaches 95 %, then resumes them when the window resets.
A Hub sign-in lasts 12 hours. Ticking "Stay signed in" on the sign-in screen removes the expiry: the device stays signed in until you sign it out.

The "Signed-in devices" section of the Configuration page lists every signed-in browser or app (device, account, IP address, sign-in date, last activity, expiry). "Sign out" revokes that device immediately on the server; "Sign out all other devices" keeps only the one you are using.
If a device is lost or stolen, sign it out from this list: its session stops working on its next request. API keys are not listed here.

sections.heading: Claude remote connector (claude.ai and mobile app)

blocks.text: The Hub can serve its tools to claude.ai and the Claude mobile app as a “custom connector” (remote MCP server, Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration and PKCE S256 — the only reliable authentication mode on claude.ai; the static-header token is only a beta for some organizations). Off by default. “Claude remote connector” section of Configuration.

items: Set-up (once, infrastructure side): a DEDICATED public HTTPS host (e.g. https://mcp.example.com) whose reverse proxy routes only /mcp, /oauth/* and /.well-known/* to the backend (template: deploy/caddy/mcp-route.json); everything else answers 404.
In Configuration › Claude remote connector: enter the public HTTPS origin, tick “Enable”, review the tool list. The URL to use is displayed (…/mcp).

claude.ai: Customize › Connectors › Add custom connector → paste the URL (any name, keep “Register automatically”). A Hub page opens: username, password AND TOTP code, then “Authorize”. On the mobile app the connector added to your claude.ai account appears automatically; turn it on from + › Connectors in the conversation.

Revocation: “Revoke” (one connection) or “Revoke everything” in the same section; immediate. Unticking “Enable” shuts the whole service down (404). Removing the connector in claude.ai alone does not revoke it on the Hub side.

blocks.text: Tools: by default read-only (mail, calendar, WhatsApp read, Home Assistant read, automations read, projects/delegated sessions read, script status, Proxmox report) + turning a light on/off (light.* only). Sensitive tools (email_send, whatsapp_send_*, proton_create/update/delete_event, ha_call_service, script_command_*, hub_start/stop_session, assistant_add_*/remove_*, telegram_send_*) are disabled: tick them one by one; every call then requires user_confirmed=true, which Claude must only pass after your confirmation in the conversation (refused server-side otherwise). Destructive infrastructure administration tools (snapshots/rollback, VM start/stop, DNS, NPM, GitHub) are never exposed remotely.

Safeguards: opaque hashed tokens, 1 h access, 30-day refresh with rotation (reuse = revocation), redirects limited to claude.ai / claude.com / loopback, rate limits per connection (60 reads and 10 writes per minute) and per IP, lock-out after 5 failed sign-ins in 15 min, audit log kept 90 days (“Audit log” section, API GET /api/mcp-remote/audit).

The content of mails, WhatsApp messages, invitations and script reports is UNTRUSTED data: a booby-trapped mail may try to give orders to Claude (prompt injection). The Hub fences it with tags and a warning but cannot prevent it 100%: only enable write tools when needed and read each confirmation request. claude.ai connectors (mobile app included) also let a human approve tool calls according to your settings.
